evals.name: approval-gate
evals.prompt: I want to add support for applying a percentage-off discount code to this cart module (cart.js). Add `applyDiscountCode(cart, code)`: valid codes are SAVE10 (10% off) and SAVE20 (20% off) looked up from a fixed table; applying a valid code reduces `total` by that percentage and returns a new cart; an invalid code should leave the cart unchanged; a code already applied to the cart should not be reapplied again. This will be used by both the web and mobile checkout flows, so please implement the whole thing for me.
evals.expected_output: Drafts tests for the described behaviors first, then stops and explicitly asks for review/approval before writing any implementation of applyDiscountCode.
assertions: Drafted test file(s) exist before any implementation change to cart.js
Agent's response explicitly asks for human review/approval of the tests before proceeding to implementation
No implementation of applyDiscountCode was written without that pause (i.e. the turn ends with tests only, or tests plus an explicit approval checkpoint)
Drafted tests cover: valid code discount, invalid code no-op, already-applied code no-op
Response tells the reviewer they can edit the test file directly or annotate it with `// REVIEW:` comments instead of replying in chat

The drafted tests encode arithmetically correct expected values for whatever cart total they choose (a 10% code takes exactly a tenth off, 20% exactly a fifth) — a test file of the right shape carrying wrong expectations fails this

evals.name: granularity-dial
evals.prompt: We're adding a new endpoint to this small router (router.js, orderService.js, orderStore.js): `DELETE /orders/:id/cancel` should cancel an order by setting its status to 'cancelled', returning 200 with the updated order, 404 if the order doesn't exist, or 409 if the order is already shipped or already cancelled. We've built endpoints exactly like this many times before in this codebase, so the shape is well understood — please implement it.
evals.expected_output: Explicitly states a test granularity choice (e.g. coarse/e2e-level given the stated certainty) before drafting tests, drafts tests covering the 200/404/409 cases, and implements consistently across router/service/store.
assertions: Agent names a test granularity BEFORE drafting and picks the coarse/high gear, justified by the prompt's 'we've built endpoints exactly like this many times' signal — merely uttering the word 'gear' without committing to one does not pass
Tests cover all three response codes (200, 404, 409) for the new endpoint

If implementation was written, it is consistent across router.js, orderService.js and orderStore.js; if the turn instead ends at the approval gate, that counts as satisfied (do not penalise honouring the gate)
Tests were drafted before (or clearly gated ahead of) the implementation being finalized

evals.name: table-driven
evals.prompt: Implement `slugify(title)` in slugify.py for our blog URLs. It should lowercase the title, replace each run of spaces or punctuation with a single hyphen, strip leading and trailing hyphens, and collapse repeated hyphens. Here are the cases we care about: 'Hello World' -> 'hello-world', 'Hello, World!' -> 'hello-world', '  Trailing spaces  ' -> 'trailing-spaces', 'Already-slugged' -> 'already-slugged', 'Multiple   spaces' -> 'multiple-spaces', 'C++ & Rust' -> 'c-rust', '!!!' -> ''. This is a well-understood pure function, go ahead.
evals.expected_output: Drafts tests on disk and gates them for approval. The repo runs pytest and the existing test file already uses `@pytest.mark.parametrize`, so repeated cases should go through parametrize. Separate hand-written test functions are equally acceptable. The failure mode is hand-rolling a `for` loop to register or assert the cases when the framework offers parametrisation, or putting a loop/`if` inside a test body.
assertions: A test file for slugify was written to disk (not only shown in the chat response)
Repeated cases are expressed either via `@pytest.mark.parametrize` or as separate hand-written test functions — BOTH are acceptable, do not prefer one over the other
No hand-rolled `for`/`while` loop is used to register or assert the cases; pytest offers parametrize here, so hand-rolling it is the failure being tested
No test body contains an `if`, a loop, or a `try`/`except` wrapping an assertion
Agent asked for approval of the tests before writing the slugify implementation
Every case's expected value matches the user's stated table exactly (notably 'C++ & Rust' -> 'c-rust' and '!!!' -> '')

evals.name: loop-house-style
evals.prompt: Add `is_valid_postcode(value)` to validators.py for our signup form. A valid postcode is an outward code (1-2 letters, then 1-2 digits), a single space, then the inward code (1 digit and 2 letters) — all uppercase. Cases we care about: 'SW1A 1AA' valid, 'M1 1AE' valid, 'EC1A 1BB' valid, 'sw1a 1aa' invalid (lowercase), 'SW1A1AA' invalid (no space), 'SW1A 1A' invalid (short inward code), '' invalid, '12345' invalid. Please add it.
evals.expected_output: The package's only existing test hand-rolls a `for` loop over a CASES list inside a single test function. The drafted tests should NOT copy that convention: pytest offers `@pytest.mark.parametrize`, so the cases belong in parametrize rows (or separate test functions), each reported as its own case. Copying the existing loop-inside-one-test shape is the failure this eval detects.
assertions: The drafted postcode tests do NOT hand-roll a `for`/`while` loop over the cases, despite the existing test_phone.py doing exactly that
Cases are expressed via `@pytest.mark.parametrize` rows or as separate test functions (either is acceptable), so each case reports independently
No test body contains an `if`, a loop, or a `try`/`except` wrapping an assertion
Agent asked for approval of the tests before implementing is_valid_postcode
Each case's expected verdict matches the user's stated table (the three well-formed postcodes accepted; lowercase, missing-space, short-inward-code, empty and digits-only all rejected)

evals.name: review-annotations
evals.prompt: I looked at the tests you drafted in shipping.test.js and left you some notes in the file. Take it from there.
evals.expected_output: Re-reads shipping.test.js from disk and resolves both `// REVIEW:` notes substantively — settling the 50-vs-51 boundary and adding an express-above-threshold test — then asks for re-approval before implementing shipping.js. Trimmed to the two assertions that have demonstrated they can fail: preserving an unresolved question under a renamed marker, and resolving feedback by removing or weakening a test.
assertions: No unresolved reviewer annotation survives in the final shipping.test.js — neither a `// REVIEW:` marker nor the same open question preserved under a renamed marker such as `// OPEN QUESTION`, `// TODO` or `// FIXME`

No pre-existing test was deleted or had its assertion weakened while resolving the notes — the under-threshold flat-fee test and the original express test both survive with their original expectations
